motion: America is Finally Winning the War in Iraq

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: If Iraqis are increasingly carrying responsibility and America can reduce its role without abandoning them, what exactly would count as winning for you, if not a successful transfer toward self-rule?

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Today we debate the motion, America is Finally Winning the War in Iraq. Liz takes the PRO side, saying the motion is true; Bonnie takes the CON side, saying it is false. Each opening gets thirty seconds, crossfire lasts two and a half minutes, and each closing gets thirty seconds. I will give a ten-second cue.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: America is finally winning because the war's central test is no longer whether every danger has vanished, but whether Iraq is moving toward self-rule and lasting security. Violence has lost its grip, local forces are taking responsibility, and ordinary families can plan beyond the next attack. That change matters.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds from this side?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: We should not confuse a difficult transition with defeat. America helped create the conditions for Iraqis to govern themselves, and that achievement is visible even when hard problems remain. The remaining-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That's time, thank you. Bonnie, the floor is yours.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The motion says America is finally winning, but that claim demands more than a hopeful direction. Iraq remains unstable, its government depends on outside support, and violence can return whenever pressure eases. A mission that cannot secure a durable result is not a victory; it is an unfinished gamble.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that concludes round one. Now onto round two and round two is where the debaters address one another. You get two and a half minutes from the moment I finish speaking. I will give you a ten-second warning.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If America is winning, what concrete result proves it rather than merely showing that the fighting has changed? Can you name an achievement that survives when American forces and money are reduced?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your point about permanence sets an impossible standard. Winning does not mean Iraq needs no help; it means responsibility is shifting to Iraqis, and that shift is already making security more durable.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: When Iraqi institutions cannot protect citizens without American backing, withdrawal leaves a dangerous vacuum. Under that condition, apparent progress is dependence, not victory, however calm the streets look today.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I reject the premise that continued support proves America is losing; successful transitions need assistance. Iraqis are assuming security duties, and that handoff shows the strategy is working, even if the handoff is-

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Military involvement without a clear end state cannot produce lasting peace. Even when local forces improve, an open-ended mission keeps Iraq from proving that its stability belongs to its own institutions.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: America always gains security by staying engaged in Iraq. Engagement lets America protect the progress already made, train local forces, and prevent a fragile success from becoming another threat.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If engagement always brings security, why has years of engagement left Iraq vulnerable to renewed violence and political failure? What makes this same commitment a win now instead of another delay?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: America does not always gain security by staying engaged in Iraq. In Iraq, continued involvement can deepen resentment and preserve dependence rather than create the security America seeks.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: They do america always gains security by staying engaged in Iraq or they should america does not always gain security by staying engaged in Iraq?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: My first statement describes the lasting security America gains from engagement as a strategy; my second describes what a particular period of engagement can produce. A sound policy can yield a short-term setback while still protecting long-term security.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That distinction concedes my point: engagement can produce insecurity and dependence. Calling the policy a win because it might help later avoids the result Iraqis actually face, which is instability without a reliable finish.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your weakest claim is that any temporary setback defeats the strategy. That confuses an unfinished handoff with failure; progress can require patience while Iraqis build institutions strong enough to carry responsibility.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I grant that a handoff can take patience. But patience is not proof of victory, and continued dependence means America has not won the war; it has only postponed the judgment.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: About ten seconds left in the crossfire.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: It's just in time for us to go to our closing round. And Liz, you are up first on that. Your closing remarks come now, it's your turn.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: This motion turns on direction, not perfection. America is finally winning because the purpose of the war was to leave Iraq more capable of securing and governing itself, and that is what the transition now shows. Bonnie points to danger, but danger during a handoff does not cancel progress. A win can be real before every threat disappears.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, Liz.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The strongest evidence is responsibility moving from American hands to Iraqi ones. That is not surrender or delay; it is the result America needed, and it means the motion is true.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay. Go on, Bonnie.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Liz's best argument is that responsibility is shifting, but a transfer is not a victory if the receiving institutions cannot stand securely. The continuing need for American protection shows the war's result remains conditional. Progress may exist, yet progress is not the same as winning. Until Iraq can sustain peace without outside pressure, America has not finally won this war.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A hopeful direction cannot replace a durable result. America may have helped Iraq improve, but improvement leaves the central question unanswered: can Iraq stand-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'm sorry. Your time is up. Thank you very much.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you both for your thoughtful arguments. This debate is now closed.
